analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license, safety training, and background check before buying or receiving any gun.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee and expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every person in the United States to get a federal license from the Department of Justice before buying or receiving a firearm. To get a license, a person would have to pass a firearms safety course with a written test and a live-firing test, submit fingerprints, and clear a background investigation. It would also require all private gun sales to go through a licensed dealer's background check, and require sellers to report every gun transaction to the Justice Department within three business days.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been people at risk of gun violence: communities with high shooting rates, domestic violence victims, and residents worried about guns reaching people with violent histories, since the bill would have added a full background investigation, safety training, and a "danger" review before any gun purchase. States that already run similar licensing systems could have kept their own programs. Law-abiding gun buyers would have gained a clearer, uniform national standard, though at real cost in time and money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Would have made it illegal to buy or receive a firearm without a federal license requiring completed safety training — including a written test on firearms laws and hands-on firing tests — plus a background investigation, fingerprinting, and proof of identity.

Would have let the Attorney General deny a license to anyone judged a significant danger to self or others, weighing factors like a history of threats or violence, domestic violence or stalking restraining orders, animal cruelty offenses, and drug or alcohol abuse or trafficking — with the right to challenge a denial in federal district court.

Would have closed the private-sale loophole: no one could sell or transfer a gun to an unlicensed person unless a licensed dealer first took possession and ran the same background check used for retail sales.

Would have required every seller to report each gun transaction — with the identities of buyer and seller and the gun's make, model, and serial number — to the Attorney General within three business days, and would have enrolled licensees in the FBI's Rap Back service so authorities are alerted if a licensee is later arrested.
Would have allowed states with substantially similar licensing systems to run their own programs instead, and required license offices in both urban and rural areas.

analysis.who_pays: Gun buyers would bear the biggest burden: each license would have covered a single firearm and expired 30 days after issuance, so a buyer would repeat the application, training, and background check process for essentially every purchase. Firearms dealers and manufacturers would face added compliance steps and likely lower sales volume. The Justice Department and taxpayers would pay to run the licensing system, background investigations, and transaction reporting; the bill text sets no fees or funding source for any of it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun buyers, firearms dealers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Each license would have been valid for the purchase of a single firearm and expired 30 days after issuance, forcing even careful, lawful buyers through a full application cycle for every gun — a heavy friction the bill does not offset with any fast-track option.

The denial standard gives the Attorney General broad discretion to refuse a license based on factors like prior arrests or pending charges that never led to a conviction, with review only after the denial — meaning an applicant could be barred first and argue later.

The bill text specifies no fees and no funding, so the cost of training courses, licensing offices, background investigations, and a national transaction-reporting system would have landed on applicants and taxpayers in amounts left entirely to later rulemaking.

The requirement that sellers report identifying details of every transfer — buyer, seller, make, model, serial number — is the kind of transaction record that gun rights groups have long described as a de facto registry of gun ownership, the core of their objection to licensing bills like this one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety case is real: a universal license with mandatory training, a full background investigation, and a danger review before every gun purchase would be one of the strongest federal gun laws ever enacted, and the bill includes due process (judicial review of denials, a hearing within 30 days of revocation, state opt-outs). But the design is heavy-handed. A one-gun, 30-day license multiplies cost and delay for the vast majority of buyers who are never implicated in violence, the danger-denial standard leans on unconvicted arrests and executive discretion, and the bill provides no funding or fee structure. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the burden falls broadly on lawful buyers, not just on the people the danger provisions target.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the Federal Firearm Licensing Act on September 10, 2019, with Senator Richard Blumenthal and one other Democrat as cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of federal gun licensing came out ahead: the firearms industry and gun rights groups avoided a national licensing and transaction-reporting system, and gun buyers avoided a new license-per-purchase process. No one gained new protections, since the bill never became law.

against.name: National Rifle Association and gun rights organizations
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed federal gun licensing and permitting schemes as burdens on law-abiding owners, shaping the political environment that kept the bill from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all three Senate sponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee and Republican-run Senate never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have added a licensing step to every sale, forced all private transfers through a dealer's background check, and required transaction reports to the Justice Department within three business days — new compliance costs on top of likely lower sales volume. Dealers' interest in unimpeded sales runs against the bill's public-safety purpose.
A license required for each single gun purchase, expiring after 30 days, would have suppressed demand for new guns — the industry's revenue depends on units sold.
The mandatory training requirement — a written test plus hands-on firing tests — would have created a guaranteed new market of millions of prospective gun buyers needing certified instruction.
